q: What is a recurrent neural network?
short: A network that processes a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state h_t = φ(W_hh h_{t−1} + W_hx x_t + b) from one step to the next, with the same weights at every step.
detail: The hidden state is a fixed-size summary of the history; outputs o_t = W_ho h_t + b_o feed a softmax for next-token prediction. Unrolled, it's a deep network with tied weights.
example: Next-word prediction in a keyboard app.
follow: How is it trained?
Why share weights?
mistakes: Saying each time step has its own weights.

q: Why can't a feed-forward network handle sequences well?
short: Fixed input size, no memory across inputs, and no parameter sharing across positions.
detail: Padding to a maximum length wastes capacity and a pattern learnt at position 3 doesn't transfer to position 30.
example: "I grew up in France … I speak fluent ___".
follow: How do 1-D CNNs compare?
mistakes: Claiming feed-forward nets can't model order at all (they can with positional inputs, inefficiently).

q: What is parameter sharing in an RNN and why does it matter?
short: The same W_hx, W_hh, W_ho and biases are used at every time step.
detail: Fixed parameter count for any sequence length, works on unseen lengths, and generalises patterns across positions.
example: 2,661,392 parameters whether the sentence has 5 or 500 words.
follow: Where else is parameter sharing used?
mistakes: Confusing sharing across time with sharing across layers.

q: What is backpropagation through time?
short: Unroll the RNN over the sequence, run standard backprop from the last step to the first, and sum the gradients of each shared weight over all steps.
detail: ∂L/∂h_t gets a local term from ℓ_t and a term from h_{t+1}; truncated BPTT limits the window to k steps for memory and speed.
example: Training a character-level language model on 100-character chunks.
follow: Why truncate?
mistakes: Forgetting to sum over time for shared weights.

q: What is the vanishing gradient problem in RNNs?
short: Going back one step multiplies the gradient by diag(φ′)W_hh; if that factor is below 1 the gradient shrinks exponentially, so early steps get no learning signal.
detail: Factor 0.4 → 0.4²⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁸. Long-range dependencies can't be learnt. Above 1 it explodes instead.
example: Forgetting the subject of a long sentence.
follow: How do LSTMs help?
How do you fix exploding gradients?
mistakes: Blaming only the activation function.

q: GRU vs LSTM in one sentence each?
short: GRU: 2 gates (reset, update), one state, fewer parameters, faster. LSTM: 3 gates (forget, input, output) plus a separate cell state, more parameters, strongest on very long sequences.
detail: Parameters 3(hd + h² + h) vs 4(hd + h² + h). Performance is often similar; tune both.
example: GRU for an on-device model; LSTM for long audio.
follow: When would you pick a Transformer instead?
mistakes: Saying GRU has three gates.

q: What does a bidirectional RNN do and when can't you use it?
short: Runs one RNN forward and one backward and concatenates their states, so each position sees past and future context. Can't be used when the future isn't available: streaming, real-time forecasting, language generation.
detail: Doubles the recurrent computation and parameters.
example: Named-entity tagging ("I met Paris in Paris").
follow: How would you do streaming NER?
mistakes: Using a BiRNN for next-word generation.

q: Which loss trains an RNN language model?
short: Cross-entropy of the true next token under the softmax, summed (or averaged) over time steps and sequences: the negative log-likelihood.
detail: exp(average loss) = perplexity.
example: Perplexity 50 ≈ choosing between 50 equally likely words.
follow: What loss for forecasting?
mistakes: Using MSE on token indices.

q: What is the LSTM cell state?
short: A separate memory vector c_t updated additively: c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ c̃_t; the hidden state h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t) is what's exposed.
detail: The additive update gives an uninterrupted gradient path when f ≈ 1.
example: Keeping track of an open quotation mark over many tokens.
follow: Why initialise the forget bias to 1?
mistakes: Treating c_t and h_t as the same.

q: MSE vs RMSE vs MAE for forecasting?
short: MSE squares errors (penalises big misses, squared units); RMSE is its square root (target units); MAE averages absolute errors (robust to outliers, easy to read).
detail: Train with MSE, report RMSE/MAE; compare against a naïve baseline.
example: RMSE 1.8 °C for next-day temperature.
follow: Why compare with a naïve forecast?
mistakes: Reporting MSE as if it were in degrees.

q: Derive ∂L/∂h_t for a tanh RNN.
short: ∂L/∂h_t = W_ho^T(softmax(o_t) − y_t) + (∂L/∂h_{t+1}) diag(1 − h_{t+1}²) W_hh.
detail: First term: the loss at step t; second: everything h_t influenced later, through h_{t+1} = tanh(W_hh h_t + W_hx x_{t+1}). Weight gradients sum diag(1 − h_t²)·∂L/∂h_t times h_{t−1}^T (W_hh) or x_t^T (W_hx) over t.
example: Slide example: ∂L/∂h₃ = (−0.149, 0.149).
follow: Where does the vanishing factor appear?
mistakes: Dropping the future term.

q: Count the parameters of a vanilla RNN with d = 100, h = 256, V = 10,000.
detail: 96% is the output layer. GRU: 3× the recurrent part; LSTM: 4×.
example: LSTM recurrent part: 4 × 91,392 = 365,568.
follow: How do you shrink the output layer?
mistakes: Counting weights per time step.

q: Why does the GRU update gate help gradient flow?
short: h_t = z ⊙ h_{t−1} + (1 − z) ⊙ h̃_t gives ∂h_t/∂h_{t−1} ⊇ z: a path with no weight matrix or activation derivative, so with z ≈ 1 gradients pass almost unchanged.
detail: Like a residual connection through time.
example: Copying a flag across 50 steps.
follow: What does the reset gate add?
mistakes: Mixing up which value of z keeps the state (conventions differ between texts).

q: Explain the LSTM's 'constant error carousel'.
short: Because c_t = f ⊙ c_{t−1} + i ⊙ c̃_t, ∂c_t/∂c_{t−1} = f (gates fixed). With f ≈ 1 the error signal circulates through the cell without decaying.
detail: Original LSTM had no forget gate (f = 1); the forget gate (Gers 2000) lets it reset.
example: f = 0.99 keeps 0.99⁵⁰ ≈ 0.6 of the gradient over 50 steps vs 10⁻²⁰ for a vanilla factor 0.4.
follow: Why initialise b_f ≈ 1?
mistakes: Claiming LSTMs never forget.

q: Your RNN's loss suddenly becomes NaN. What happened and what do you do?
short: Probably exploding gradients. Clip the gradient norm (e.g. 1–5), lower the learning rate, use LSTM/GRU, check inputs for scale.
detail: Monitor gradient norms; orthogonal or identity-scaled W_hh initialisation; layer norm.
example: ReLU RNN on long sequences.
follow: Clipping by value vs by norm?
mistakes: Only lowering the learning rate.

q: Markov n-gram model vs RNN language model?
short: n-gram: fixed window of n − 1 words, V^n table entries, no generalisation between similar words. RNN: unbounded (in principle) context via a learnt hidden state, shared parameters, embeddings generalise.
detail: RNN still has a practical memory limit (vanishing gradients).
example: Trigram forgets 'cat' when predicting 'mat'.
follow: How does smoothing help n-grams?
mistakes: Saying RNNs have exactly infinite memory.

q: Design a next-day temperature forecaster from 7 days of temperature, humidity and pressure.
short: Multivariate input x_t ∈ ℝ³, LSTM with h = 64, read 7 steps, linear head on h₇ → one number (many-to-one), MSE loss; chronological splits; scale with training statistics; report RMSE/MAE against a 'tomorrow = today' baseline.
example: From the slides' forecasting example.
follow: How would you forecast a week ahead?
mistakes: Random train/test split that leaks the future.

q: What's the difference between deep (stacked) and bidirectional RNNs?
short: Stacked: layer ℓ's states are layer ℓ+1's inputs (hierarchy). Bidirectional: two RNNs at the same level reading opposite directions (context). They can be combined.
detail: Deep RNNs compound vanishing gradients through time and depth; 2–4 layers typical.
example: A 2-layer BiLSTM encoder.
follow: Parameter count of a 2-layer BiLSTM?
mistakes: Calling a BiRNN a 2-layer RNN.

q: Show why vanilla RNN gradients vanish or explode.
short: ∂L/∂h_1 = ∂L/∂h_T ∏ diag(φ′(z_t)) W_hh. Its norm is bounded by (max|φ′| ‖W_hh‖)^{T−1}: below 1 it decays exponentially; the largest singular value above 1 is necessary (not sufficient) for explosion.
detail: Pascanu et al. 2013. Remedies: gating, orthogonal init, clipping, skip connections, attention.
follow: Why is ‖W‖ > 1 not sufficient for explosion?
mistakes: Saying tanh always causes explosion.

q: What is teacher forcing and what is exposure bias?
short: Teacher forcing feeds the ground-truth previous token during training; at inference the model feeds its own predictions, a distribution it never trained on (exposure bias).
detail: Mitigations: scheduled sampling, sequence-level training, larger data.
example: Text generation drifting after an early mistake.
follow: How do Transformers handle this?
mistakes: Thinking teacher forcing is used at inference.

q: RNN vs Transformer for a long sequence: trade-offs?
short: RNN: O(T) sequential steps, O(h) memory at inference, natural streaming, path length T between distant tokens. Transformer: parallel over T in training, O(1) path length, but O(T²) attention and O(T) KV cache.
detail: State-space models (e.g. Mamba) combine linear-time recurrence with parallel training.
example: Streaming speech on a device vs document summarisation.
follow: What is a KV cache?
mistakes: Saying RNNs are obsolete everywhere.

q: Why initialise the LSTM forget-gate bias to ~1?
short: So σ(b_f) ≈ 0.73 at the start: the cell remembers by default and gradients flow through c from the first updates; with b_f = 0 the initial f ≈ 0.5 halves memory every step.
detail: Jozefowicz et al. 2015 found this simple change matters.
example: 0.5⁴⁰ ≈ 10⁻¹² vs 0.73⁴⁰ ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁶ (and f moves towards 1 with training).
follow: Equivalent trick for GRUs?
mistakes: Initialising all biases to zero without thought.

q: A BiLSTM tagger is great offline but you need streaming predictions with ≤200 ms delay. What do you do?
short: Use a unidirectional (causal) model, or a limited look-ahead: let the backward direction see only a small future window and emit labels with that delay; distil the BiLSTM into the causal model.
detail: Chunked bidirectional processing with overlap is another option.
example: Live captioning.
follow: How would you measure the accuracy cost?
mistakes: Running the BiLSTM on the growing prefix each time (quadratic cost).

q: Count the parameters of a 2-layer bidirectional LSTM, d = 100, h = 128 per direction, V = 10,000.
detail: Use the lab's calculator to check other configurations.
example: Framework counts may differ slightly: PyTorch uses two bias vectors per gate.
follow: Why do PyTorch counts include b_ih and b_hh?
mistakes: Using h instead of 2h as layer 2's input.
